findings.claim: "Modern prose questions on Anita and Me commonly follow a two-part format... The extract task... The wider-text task..." plus "part (a)"/"part (b)" wording in the exam tips of lessons 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 and 8, a "Two-Part Extract Question" heading, a 25+25 minute split, and all 48 practice questions labelled "20 marks - Extract Analysis" or "20 marks - Wider Text Response" with a 17-20 / 13-16 / 9-12 / 5-8 / 1-4 band ladder.
findings.truth: The post-1914 prose section is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract printed on the paper and a single answer that must also range across the novel. The two-part 20+20 pattern belongs to another board. Questions relabelled "40 marks - Source-Based Response" and the ladder rebuilt as 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8, matching the sibling Eduqas post-1914 units.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md (Component 2 Section A: 40 marks, source based, AO1/AO2/AO4, closed book; paper 2h30 for three 40-mark sections)

findings.claim: "In the Eduqas exam, AO4 assesses your ability to show understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written"; "For AO4, embed context within your analysis"; "weaving in context (AO1 + AO2 + AO4)"; a knowledge check keyed so that AO4 = "contexts"; and 14 mark schemes crediting "AO4 context".
findings.truth: Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only, and AO4 in this specification is accurate written English (vocabulary, sentence structures, spelling and punctuation). Context is NOT assessed on this question at all, so a context paragraph earns nothing. Every AO4-as-context claim rewritten; background kept only where it sharpens a point about the writing.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md (Component 2 Section A: 40 marks, source based, AO1/AO2/AO4, closed book; paper 2h30 for three 40-mark sections); spec section 3.1 AO definitions

findings.claim: "essential for the Eduqas exam", "In the Eduqas exam", "For the Eduqas exam", "the Eduqas two-part question", "Time management is critical in the Eduqas exam", plus two knowledge checks and a flashcard naming the board.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board in student-facing text. Reworded to "the exam", "your prose question", "this question".
findings.evidence: house rule (feedback_eduqas_wjec_neutral_phrasing)

findings.claim: The Empire Windrush arrived "carrying 492 passengers from the Caribbean" (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: The ship's manifest at the National Archives records 802 passengers who gave a Caribbean country as their last place of residence. The 492 figure comes from 1948 press reports and is now known to be wrong.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMT_Empire_Windrush

findings.claim: Sam Lowbridge at the fete "declares, 'If you want a nigger for a neighbour, vote Labour'" - repeated in Lesson 4 and taught as a memorisation flashcard.
findings.truth: That is the 1964 Smethwick election slogan, not a line in the novel. At the fete Sam objects to the collection going to "some darkies we've never met" and shouts "This is our patch. Not some wogs' handout." Corrected in both lessons and in the flashcard.
findings.evidence: Chapter 7 (p.193) as cited in published study notes; LitCharts plot summary of the fete scene

findings.claim: "I do not have a name for what I felt" is given as Meena's opening line and as the first item in the memorisation bank; it appears in lessons 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 (content, key facts, revision tips, knowledge checks and flashcards).
findings.truth: The novel opens "I do not have many memories of my very early childhood, apart from the obvious ones, of course." The quoted line appears in no published quotation index of the novel and looks like a garble of the Chapter 13 line "a girl with no name or no place". Replaced with the real opening line where the opening is meant, and with the Chapter 6 line "I knew I was a freak of some kind, too mouthy, clumsy and scabby to be a real Indian girl" where the point is her confusion.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quotes index p.9 and pp.149-150; GradeSaver quotes page

findings.claim: "I'm not lying, I'm just telling a story" quoted as Meena's line in lessons 2, 5 and 8, including a fill-in knowledge check and the memorisation bank.
findings.truth: The real Chapter 1 line is "I'm not really a liar, I just learned very early on that those of us deprived of history sometimes need to turn to mythology to feel complete, to belong." Corrected throughout.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quotes index p.10; GradeSaver

findings.claim: "If you can't fit in, you might as well stand out" given as Meena's concluding realisation in lessons 3, 5, 6 and 8, including two keyed knowledge-check answers and the memorisation bank.
findings.truth: No such line is in the novel; it reads as a modern slogan. Meena's closing realisation is "the place in which I belonged was wherever I stood and there was nothing stopping me simply moving forward". Corrected throughout.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character analysis of Meena Kumar (ending); Chapter 13

findings.claim: "This is also my home" given as Meena's line near the end in lessons 5, 6 and 8, including a fill-in knowledge check.
findings.truth: Not in the novel. The closing sentence has Meena "claiming each resting place as home". Corrected; the knowledge check still keys "home".
findings.evidence: Chapter 13 closing sentence as quoted in published study notes

findings.claim: "Anita's father is entirely absent"; Deirdre is "a single mother"; and (Lesson 6) Deirdre is trapped by "the absence of Anita's father".
findings.truth: The reverse is true. Anita's father is present and raises Anita and Tracey; it is Deirdre who runs off with a butcher halfway through the novel and leaves Tollington. Corrected in both lessons.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character page for Deirdre; GradeSaver character list

findings.claim: "This demonstrates sophisticated understanding for AO1 and AO2."
findings.truth: The house validator rejects an assessment code written immediately before a full stop. Reworded to "...of the text (AO1) and of Syal's methods (AO2)."
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md validator limits

findings.claim: "code-switch" is defined as "A form of speech or writing that says one thing but means another, often used for humour or social commentary."
findings.truth: That is the definition of irony. Code-switching is moving between two languages or dialects depending on who you are speaking to - which is what the lesson goes on to describe. Corrected in the glossary and in the matching dfn attribute.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 of the same unit defines the term correctly

findings.claim: "Meena wins a scholarship to a grammar school", repeated in the lesson description, conclusion, a knowledge check, two flashcards, a mark scheme and Lesson 8.
findings.truth: Meena passes the eleven-plus and wins a grammar school place; the novel does not award her a scholarship. Reworded.
findings.evidence: LitCharts plot summary (eleven-plus); brief's plot facts

findings.claim: "Papa (Kumar)" set against "Mama (Daljit)".
findings.truth: Papa's given name is Shyam Kumar, so the bracket gave a surname where the parallel gave a first name.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver character list

findings.claim: "We are the British" is attributed to Papa in lessons 1, 2, 6 and 8, keyed as a fill-in knowledge check answer, set as a flashcard to memorise, and named in a mark scheme.
findings.truth: I could not find this line in any published quotation index (LitCharts, GradeSaver, Goodreads, Save My Exams), including the Papa-specific lists, so it is probably fabricated - but the text is in copyright and I could not search it, so I have not edited it. OPTIONS: (a) replace every instance with a verified line about belonging, for example Meena's "the place in which I belonged was wherever I stood", and re-point the knowledge check and flashcard at that; (b) keep it if Tom or a copy of the novel can confirm the wording. Recommendation: (a) - a memorisation card is the worst place for an unverified quotation.
findings.evidence: absent from LitCharts quote index, GradeSaver quotes, Goodreads quotes and Save My Exams character quotations

findings.claim: "I wanted to be them. I wanted their life" is quoted as Meena's line about the Rutter sisters in lessons 2, 3, 5 and 8, including a keyed knowledge check and two flashcards.
findings.truth: Unverified. Published sources give "I wanted to be Anita Rutter more than I had ever wanted anything in my life" for this moment, but only from a site whose quotation list looks unreliable, so I have not edited it. OPTIONS: (a) replace with the wording above once someone can check page 1 of Chapter 2 against a copy; (b) drop the quotation marks and paraphrase. Recommendation: (a).
findings.evidence: not in LitCharts or GradeSaver quote indexes

findings.claim: Meena describes feeling "connected to something enormous and ancient" (lessons 4 and 8).
findings.truth: Not verifiable in any published quotation index. It is used as description rather than as a memorisation target, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: absent from LitCharts and GradeSaver quote indexes

findings.claim: The unit dates the story inconsistently: "looking back on the 1960s" (lessons 1 and 5), "depicting the late 1960s" (Lesson 5 flashcard) and "1970s Britain" (Lesson 6 flashcard).
findings.truth: Sources disagree: Wikipedia says the late 1960s, LitCharts says the 1970s, and most teaching notes put the action around 1972. No claim is demonstrably wrong, so nothing is edited, but the unit should settle on one form of words.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Anita and Me (novel)'; LitCharts plot summary

findings.claim: "This is verbal irony on a structural level - the whole novel says one thing on the surface and means something more complex underneath."
findings.truth: The effect described (the reader understanding more than the narrator) is dramatic irony, which the same lesson defines correctly two paragraphs earlier. Left alone because the glossary entry itself is right and an edit would strand the term.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 glossary entries for dramatic irony and verbal irony

findings.claim: Meena's Black Country dialect is illustrated with "yow" and "bostin".
findings.truth: Both are genuine Black Country words but I could not confirm that either appears in the novel. Not edited.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: A knowledge check keys "Harmonium" as the instrument Papa plays, and the content says he "plays the harmonium".
findings.truth: Published summaries confirm Papa leads mehfils and sings ghazals, but none names the instrument. Plausible and not edited; worth a check against a copy of the novel.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Chapter 4 summary (mehfil, ghazals)

findings.claim: Tollington is "a thinly disguised version of the real Black Country mining village of Essington in the West Midlands".
findings.truth: Essington is a mining village in South Staffordshire, a few miles north of Wolverhampton, on the northern edge of the Black Country rather than inside it. Defensible as written (it is in the West Midlands region) so not edited.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meera_Syal

summary: All eight lessons carried the wrong exam format (a two-part 20+20 extract/wider-text question with AO4 defined as context) and four fabricated 'key quotations' that the unit told students to memorise; the novel's opening line, Meena's line about lying, her closing realisation and Sam Lowbridge's fete words were all wrong, and Anita's father and Deirdre's marriage were reversed. 207 edits fix the format, the band ladder, the AO4 definition, the verified quotations and the plot facts; 'We are the British' and 'I wanted to be them' are flagged for adjudication because the text is in copyright and I could not disprove them.
